title: Linked List Cycle
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether a singly linked list contains a cycle, without modifying the list.
Idea: Move slow one node at a time and fast two nodes at a time. If they ever reference the same node, a cycle exists; if fast reaches null, the list is acyclic.
Technique and why it applies: Inside a cycle, the faster pointer gains one node per iteration on the slower pointer, so they must eventually meet.
Invariant: If the list has no cycle, fast eventually reaches the end; a meeting can only occur when nodes repeat in a cycle.
Edge cases: Empty and one-node acyclic lists return false. Compare node identity, not node values.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Both pointers advance at fixed speeds without storing visited nodes.

title: Linked List Cycle II
approach_name: Find meeting point then cycle entrance
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the exact node where a linked-list cycle begins, or null if the list has no cycle. Do not modify the list.
Idea: First use Floyd's slow/fast pointers to find a meeting inside the cycle. If they meet, reset one pointer to the head and advance both one step at a time; their next meeting is the cycle entrance.
Technique and why it applies: The distance relationship between the head-to-entry prefix and the cycle's remaining distance makes the reset pointers meet at the entry.
Invariant: The first phase establishes that a cycle exists; the second phase converges on its first node.
Edge cases: An acyclic list returns null. A cycle may begin at the head, and a one-node self-cycle is valid.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Floyd's meeting and entrance phases use only two pointers.

title: Reorder List
approach_name: Split, reverse second half, and weave
notes:
Task and constraints: Reorder a list L0,L1,...,Ln as L0,Ln,L1,Ln-1,... without changing node values.
Idea: Find the midpoint with slow/fast pointers, detach and reverse the second half, then alternate nodes from the first and reversed second halves.
Technique and why it applies: The reversed second half places the original final node first, allowing a simple alternating merge to produce the required order.
Invariant: During weaving, the first list holds the next front node and the reversed list holds the next back node to insert.
Edge cases: Lists of length one or two need no special reordering. Detach the halves before reversing to avoid cycles.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Midpoint search, reversal, and weaving each traverse a linear portion of the list.
code:
from typing import Optional

class Solution:
    def reorderList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> None:
        if not head or not head.next:return
        slow=fast=head
        while fast.next and fast.next.next:slow=slow.next;fast=fast.next.next
        cur=slow.next;slow.next=None;prev=None
        while cur:nxt=cur.next;cur.next=prev;prev=cur;cur=nxt
        first,second=head,prev
        while second:
            a,b=first.next,second.next;first.next=second;second.next=a;first=a;second=b

title: Binary Tree Preorder Traversal
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the preorder traversal of a binary tree: visit the node, then its left subtree, then its right subtree.
Idea: Use a stack. Pop and record a node, push its right child first, then its left child so the left child is processed next.
Technique and why it applies: A LIFO stack reverses push order, allowing the iterative traversal to match root-left-right recursion.
Invariant: The output is the preorder prefix already visited, and the stack holds pending subtrees in reverse processing order.
Edge cases: An empty tree returns an empty list. Push right before left to preserve the required order.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(h) to O(n), depending on tree shape.
complexity_reason: Every node is pushed and popped once.

title: Binary Tree Postorder Traversal
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the postorder traversal of a binary tree: left subtree, right subtree, then node.
Idea: Perform an iterative root-right-left traversal by pushing left before right, collect values, then reverse the collected sequence.
Technique and why it applies: Reversing root-right-left yields left-right-root, exactly the postorder order.
Invariant: Before reversal, the collected list follows root-right-left; after reversal, it follows left-right-root.
Edge cases: Empty trees return an empty list. The method uses an explicit stack rather than recursive calls.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(n) for the stack and output list.
complexity_reason: The stack and collected traversal each store up to n nodes/values.

title: Insertion Sort List
approach_name: Insert each node into sorted prefix
notes:
Task and constraints: Sort a singly linked list in ascending order using insertion sort.
Idea: Maintain a sorted list behind a dummy head. Remove each node from the input and insert it after the last sorted node whose value is less than or equal to it; if that shortcut fails, search from the dummy head.
Technique and why it applies: Insertion sort maintains a sorted prefix and inserts each next element into its correct position.
Invariant: The nodes before the unsorted pointer form a sorted list containing exactly the nodes already processed.
Edge cases: Duplicate values are handled by inserting after existing equals. Empty and one-node lists are already sorted.
Complexity: Worst-case time is O(n^2). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Each node is inserted into the sorted prefix using only pointer updates.
code:
from typing import Optional

class Solution:
    def insertionSortList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        dummy=ListNode(0);cur=head;tail=dummy
        while cur:
            nxt=cur.next
            if tail is dummy or tail.val<=cur.val:prev=tail
            else:
                prev=dummy
                while prev.next and prev.next.val<=cur.val:prev=prev.next
            cur.next=prev.next;prev.next=cur
            if cur.val>=tail.val if tail is not dummy else True:tail=cur
            cur=nxt
        return dummy.next

title: Sort List
notes:
Task and constraints: Sort a linked list in ascending order in O(n log n) time.
Idea: Split the list into halves using slow/fast pointers, recursively sort each half, and merge the two sorted lists with a dummy head.
Technique and why it applies: Merge sort works well on linked lists because splitting and merging need only sequential pointer traversal, not random access.
Invariant: Each recursive call returns a sorted list containing exactly the nodes from its input segment.
Edge cases: Empty and single-node lists are already sorted. Break the list at the midpoint before recursive calls.
Complexity: Time is O(n log n). Extra space is O(log n) for recursive calls.
complexity_reason: Each merge level processes all n nodes and there are logarithmically many levels.
code:
from typing import Optional

class Solution:
    def sortList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        if not head or not head.next:return head
        slow,fast=head,head.next
        while fast and fast.next:slow=slow.next;fast=fast.next.next
        mid=slow.next;slow.next=None
        a=self.sortList(head);b=self.sortList(mid)
        dummy=ListNode(0);tail=dummy
        while a and b:
            if a.val<=b.val:tail.next=a;a=a.next
            else:tail.next=b;b=b.next
            tail=tail.next
        tail.next=a or b
        return dummy.next

title: Max Points on a Line
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the maximum number of points that lie on one straight line. Coordinates may repeat, and duplicate points must be counted.
Idea: For each anchor point, count other points by normalized slope. Divide the coordinate difference by its greatest common divisor and normalize the sign so equal lines share one key; count duplicates separately.
Technique and why it applies: Every line through a fixed anchor is uniquely identified by its reduced slope, with special handling for coincident points.
Invariant: The largest slope bucket plus duplicates and the anchor is the largest collinear set through that anchor.
Edge cases: Vertical and horizontal lines need canonical slope keys. Duplicate coordinates have zero difference and must not be divided by gcd zero.
Complexity: Time is O(n^2) expected. Extra space is O(n) per anchor.
complexity_reason: Each anchor compares against all later points and stores reduced slopes.
code:
from typing import List
from math import gcd

class Solution:
    def maxPoints(self, points: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        n=len(points)
        if n<=2:return n
        best=0
        for i in range(n):
            slopes={};duplicates=0;local=0
            for j in range(i+1,n):
                dx=points[j][0]-points[i][0];dy=points[j][1]-points[i][1]
                if dx==0 and dy==0:duplicates+=1;continue
                g=gcd(dx,dy);dx//=g;dy//=g
                if dx<0:dx=-dx;dy=-dy
                elif dx==0:dy=1
                key=(dy,dx);slopes[key]=slopes.get(key,0)+1;local=max(local,slopes[key])
            best=max(best,local+duplicates+1)
        return best

title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
approach_name: Evaluate operators with an operand stack
notes:
Task and constraints: Evaluate a valid reverse Polish notation expression containing integer operands and binary operators +, -, *, and /; division truncates toward zero.
Idea: Push operands. When an operator appears, pop the right operand then the left operand, apply the operator in that order, and push the result.
Technique and why it applies: In postfix notation, each operator follows its operands, so a stack holds the values waiting for an operation.
Invariant: After processing a token prefix, the stack contains the intermediate values represented by that prefix.
Edge cases: Subtraction and division are not commutative, so operand order matters. Python must implement truncation toward zero without floating-point conversion.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(n) for the operand stack.
complexity_reason: Each token is pushed or popped a constant number of times.
